findings.summary: Claims a 1-unit increase in log(income) is approximately a 100% increase in income, but the delta-ln percentage approximation is only valid for small changes; the exact effect of a 1-unit log increase is 171.8%.
findings.old: 2. **Percentage interpretation**: A 1-unit increase in log(income) ≈ 100% increase in income
findings.new: 2. **Percentage interpretation**: Small changes in log(income) are approximately percentage changes — a 0.05 increase in log(income) ≈ 5% increase in income (accurate only for small changes; a full 1-unit increase multiplies income by e ≈ 2.72; see Chapter 9)
findings.evidence: Computed: 100×(e^1 − 1) = 171.8%, not 100%. Brief Lens A canonical (ch09 §9.2): approximation accurate for |β|<0.1. The chapter contradicts itself 13 lines later (L1055: 'Difference of 1 in log scale = 2.72× in dollar scale').
findings.verify_note: Real error. A 1-unit ln increase multiplies income by e (=+171.83%), not +100%; the delta-ln≈%change rule holds only for |Δ|<0.1 (Δln=0.05→exact 5.13%). Contradicts L1055 ('2.72× in dollar scale'). Proposed replacement is accurate and pedagogically sound.

findings.new: # Positive kurtosis (>0) indicates heavy tails (extreme municipalities) — pandas .kurtosis() reports excess kurtosis

Executed values (dump cell 19) are clearly on the excess scale: imds 1.179, index_sdg1 −0.642, sdg1_1_ubn −0.030, ln_NTLpc2017 0.571 — under the '>3' rule none would count as heavy-tailed. Contradicts the chapter's own guideline at L308–311 (excess kurtosis > 0 = leptokurtic).
findings.verify_note: Verified: pandas Series.kurtosis() returns Fisher/excess kurtosis (baseline 0; ~0.008 on normal). Dump cell 19 values (imds 1.179, index_sdg1 -0.642, sdg1_1_ubn -0.030, ln_NTLpc2017 0.571) are all <3 yet imds is leptokurtic. The '>3' threshold is the raw-kurtosis rule; correct is >0. findings.summary: The 68% rule is applied to strongly right-skewed earnings without the normality qualifier, and the stated share is empirically wrong for this sample (actual: 74.9%).

findings.new: - **Rule of thumb (for bell-shaped data):** about 68% of observations fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean — here \$41,413 ± \$25,527 = \$15,886 to \$66,940. Because these earnings are right-skewed, the actual share in this band is higher: about 75%

The empirical rule presumes approximate normality, as the chapter's own Key Takeaways states at L1309 ('for normal distributions, ~68% ... within 1 standard deviation'), and this section itself stresses the data are highly skewed (skewness 1.71).

findings.summary: 'Each 1-unit increase in log(earnings) ≈ 2.718× increase in earnings' conflates a 2.718-fold multiplication with a '2.718× increase' (which reads as +271.8%); the correct statement is that earnings are multiplied by e.

findings.summary: Cheat-sheet comment claims an 11-month moving average 'cancels one full seasonal cycle', but an 11-month window does not span the 12-month seasonal cycle and cannot cancel it exactly.
findings.old: # cancels one full seasonal cycle, revealing the underlying trend
findings.new: # smooths away most of the 12-month seasonal swing, revealing the underlying trend
findings.evidence: A monthly seasonal cycle has period 12; an 11-month centered MA attenuates a period-12 component by a factor of |sin(11π/12)/(11·sin(π/12))| ≈ 0.09 (≈91% removed), i.e., strong smoothing but not full cancellation — a 12-month MA would be required for that.
findings.verify_note: Verified: an 11-pt MA attenuates a period-12 seasonal component by factor 0.0909 (90.9% removed, not fully cancelled); only a 12-pt MA gives exact cancellation (factor 0). 'Cancels one full seasonal cycle' is imprecise; 'smooths away most of the 12-month seasonal swing' is accurate.
